titleStmt.title: To Harriet Shaw Weaver. Monday, 13 November 1922
titleStmt.author: James Joyce

seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p: Dear Miss Weaver: I left Nice yesterday. I received a long, very unpleasant and very rude letter from Miss Beach about the second edition but am not replying to it until I have tested the ground there first. Her letter is, I think, unreasonable but I shall try to smooth matters over as much as possible though I should prefer some other occupation at present. It seems the Paris pot cannot be left for more than three weeks by me but it begins to boil over.

I shall reserve what I wanted to tell you about my eyes except to say that my Nice doctor (to whom of course I am presenting my novel in French) is one of the best I ever had. He attaches no importance to abscesses or glands. He diagnosed my case as rheumatic and stopped an attack of iritis in three days by the use of salicylate of soda in very large doses. I never met a doctor before who was able to do that. He considers I ought to be operated in six weeks (if I don’t get a relapse) and is writing to Dr Borsch about my case, suggesting the use of a drug called dionine to clear the nebula somewhat in the meantime. Such therefore is the moral and physical situation. Please do not allude to my first paragraph in your correspondence with Miss Beach.

postscript.p: P.S. My Paris address in case the telegram was wrong is 26 Avenue Charles Floquet Paris VII

div.note: This exchange marks a conflict between Sylvia Beach and JJ regarding the publication of the Egoist Press edition of Ulysses. Ellmann attributes their quarrel to JJ’s “daily importunities during the last year” but more specifically cites his request for publication of a third edition of Ulysses and recommendation that Beach seek reviews for the novel. Beach let JJ know she would not be “hustling to boom the book” now that the similarity between the first and second editions of Ulysses might subject her to court action ( JJ 541). Or, in JJ’s words in a 17 November 1922 letter to Weaver, Beach “went on to say that she had been kept in the dark about the second edition or misled or misinformed that it was sold out, not sold out, that there was to be a third edition, that there was not to be a third edition for a year, that the third edition was nearly ready etc.” ( LI 195-6).
Dr Louis Colin treated JJ in Nice, applying leeches and dionine solution (salicylate of soda, as JJ references later in this letter) to his eyes.

As per New York endocrinologist Dr Louis Berman’s advice in July 1922 and Dr Borsch’s similar recommendation in October 1922, JJ would undergo complete dental extraction and a subsequent sphincterectomy (the excision of a portion of the pupillary border of the iris) in early 1923. With Dr Borsch’s consent, JJ ultimately postponed the operation. On 4 April 1923, six or seven of JJ’s decayed teeth were extracted, with the rest of them a few days later. After his seventeen tooth extractions, Borsch performed a sphincterectomy in three parts (April 3, 15, and 26). Able to read better by June and with a new set of dental plates, JJ was in far better condition ( JJ 536-7; 543).
